claim: 90% of obese patients in the United States have NAFLD ranging from hepatic steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which can induce fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: Many reports have demonstrated that 90% of obese patients in the United States have NAFLD ranging from hepatic steatosis to much more severe forms of non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which can induce fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Corey and Kaplan, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Corey and Kaplan, 2014, indicating it is based on published research.

claim: NAFLD is associated with hepatic metabolic reprogramming that leads to excessive lipid accumulation and imbalances in lipid metabolism in the liver.
source: NAFLD is associated with hepatic metabolic reprogramming that leads to excessive lipid accumulation and imbalances in lipid metabolism in the liver (de Alwis and Day, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Alwis and Day, 2008.

claim: Hepatic lipid homeostasis involves signaling and transcriptional pathways, as well as targeted genes associated with fatty acid (FA) oxidation and lipogenesis.
source: Hepatic lipid homeostasis is appropriately described as a complex machinery involving signaling and transcriptional pathways, as well as targeted genes associated with fatty acid (FA) oxidation and lipogenesis (Fabbrini et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fabbrini et al., 2010.

claim: Nuclear receptors (NRs) are a superfamily of ligand-activated transcription factors that regulate biological homeostasis.
source: Nuclear receptors (NRs) are a superfamily of ligand-activated transcription factors that regulate biological homeostasis (McKenna et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McKenna et al., 2009.

claim: NRs are key regulators in the progression of diverse hepatic diseases associated with glucose and lipid metabolism, inflammation, bile acid homeostasis, fibrosis, and cancer development in the liver.
source: Recent evidence suggests that NRs are key regulators in the progression of diverse hepatic diseases associated with glucose and lipid metabolism, inflammation, bile acid homeostasis, fibrosis, and cancer development in the liver (López-Velázquez et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to López-Velázquez et al., 2012.

claim: Hepatic PPARα plays an important role in energy homeostasis by regulating the expression of genes required for FA uptake, FA oxidation, and triglyceride (TG) hydrolysis in the liver.
source: Hepatic PPARα plays an important role in energy homeostasis by regulating the expression of genes required for FA uptake, FA oxidation, and triglyceride (TG) hydrolysis in the liver (Chakravarthy et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chakravarthy et al., 2005.

claim: The decreased expression of PPARα is significantly associated with severity in NAFLD patients.
source: The decreased expression of PPARα is significantly associated with severity in NAFLD patients (Francque et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Francque et al., 2015.

claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short, non-coding RNA molecules with a length of 18–25 nucleotides that play an important role in regulating the expression of target genes in a post-transcriptional manner.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short, non-coding RNA molecules with a length of 18–25 nucleotides that play an important role in regulating the expression of target genes in a post-transcriptional manner by targeting base-pairing with the 3'UTR of specific target mRNAs, inhibiting translation, or mRNA degradation (Bartel, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bartel, 2004.

claim: miRNAs significantly regulate the pathogenesis of NAFLD by targeting the nuclear receptors.
source: Recent studies have suggested that miRNAs significantly regulate the pathogenesis of NAFLD by targeting the nuclear receptors (López-Sánchez et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to López-Sánchez et al., 2021.

claim: MIR20B, a member of the MIR17 family, presents in the circulating plasma of NAFLD patients and has been highlighted as a novel biomarker of NAFLD and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) for the diagnosis and risk estimation of NAFLD.
source: Previous report has demonstrated that MIR20B, a member of the MIR17 family, presents in the circulating plasma of NAFLD patients and has been highlighted as a novel biomarker of NAFLD and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) for the diagnosis and risk estimation of NAFLD (Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ye et al., 2018.

claim: MIR20B was prioritized as a key regulator in NAFLD through analysis of regulatory networks of miRNAs for NR genes and RNA-seq data in NAFLD patients.
source: In this study, we analyzed the regulatory networks of miRNAs for NR genes and RNA-seq data in NAFLD patients, which prioritized MIR20B as a key regulator in NAFLD.
evidence: The claim is based on the study's own analysis of regulatory networks and RNA-seq data.

claim: The expression of MIR20B was significantly increased in simple steatosis and NASH compared to that in normal individuals.
source: Among the selected miRNAs, the expression of MIR20B was significantly increased in simple steatosis and NASH compared to that in normal individuals, and the extent of increase in NASH was higher than that in simple steatosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B showing MIR20B expression levels in patient samples.

claim: The expression of MIR20B showed a significant correlation with the BMI, AST, ALT, and fasting glucose during NAFLD progression.
source: In particular, the expression of MIR20B showed a significant correlation with the BMI, AST, ALT, and fasting glucose during NAFLD progression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MIR20B expression was most significantly increased in both oleic acid (OA)-treated HepG2 and Huh-7 cells.
source: MIR20B expression was also most significantly increased in both oleic acid (OA)-treated HepG2 and Huh-7 cells (Figure 1C and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: The expression of MIR20B was significantly upregulated in the fatty livers of high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, Lepob/ob mice, and methionine-deficient diet (MCD)-fed mice compared to that in the liver of normal chow diet (NCD)-fed wild mice.
source: Moreover, the expression of MIR20B was significantly upregulated in the fatty livers of high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, Lepob/ob mice, and methionine-deficient diet (MCD)-fed mice compared to that in the liver of normal chow diet (NCD)-fed wild mice (Figure 1E–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models shown in Figures 1E-G and supplementary figures.

claim: MIR20B expression increased intracellular lipid content in HepG2 cells.
source: Oil Red O staining showed that MIR20B expression increased intracellular lipid content, and this lipid accumulation was increased with OA treatment in HepG2 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpression of MIR20B significantly upregulated TG content and cholesterol in OA-treated HepG2 cells.
source: As expected, overexpression of MIR20B significantly upregulated TG content and cholesterol in OA-treated HepG2 cells (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The NR metapathway was detected as the most significant pathways (adjusted p-value = 2.47-E8) by the gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
source: The NR metapathway was detected as the most significant pathways (adjusted p-value = 2.47-E8) by the gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005), indicating that NRs and related genes are the major targets of MIR20B (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis results shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: PPARA was the most significantly downregulated NR (adjusted p-value = 3.25-E5) among five NRs (PPARA, RORA, RORC, THRB, and NRBP1) that were downregulated.
source: Five NRs (PPARA, RORA, RORC, THRB, and NRBP1) were downregulated (adjusted p-value ≤ 0.05), and PPARA was the most significantly downregulated NR (adjusted p-value = 3.25-E5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis data.

claim: PPARA pathways and PPAR signaling pathways were significantly decreased in MIR20B overexpressed cells.
source: Furthermore, GSEA showed that PPARA pathways and PPAR signaling pathways were significantly decreased in MIR20B overexpressed cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The expression change of PPARA at both the protein and mRNA levels with MIR20B transfection was the most distinct compared to the control.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data, the expression change of PPARA at both the protein and mRNA levels with MIR20B transfection was the most distinct compared to the control (Figure 2H1).
evidence: The claim is supported by protein and mRNA expression data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: PPARA was selected as an overlapped predicted target of MIR20B between various miRNA target prediction programs, including miRDB, picTAR, TargetSCAN, and miRmap.
source: Moreover, among candidate targets from RNA-seq analysis, only PPARA was selected as an overlapped predicted target of MIR20B between various miRNA target prediction programs, including miRDB, picTAR, TargetSCAN, and miRmap (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PPARA significantly decreased as NAFLD progressed to steatosis and NASH, and showed a negative correlation with that of MIR20B.
source: While the expression of other candidates, including RORA, RORC, and THRB, remained unchanged, that of PPARA significantly decreased as NAFLD progressed to steatosis and NASH, and showed a negative correlation with that of MIR20B (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression and correlation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The 3'UTR of PPARA mRNA includes MIR20B binding sites that are well conserved between humans and mice.
source: Notably, the 3'UTR of PPARA mRNA includes MIR20B binding sites that are well conserved between humans and mice, suggesting that MIR20B may have a direct inhibitory effect on PPARA expression (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: MIR20B suppressed the luciferase activity in both HepG2 and Huh-7 cells in a dose-dependent manner using a luciferase reporter construct including the 3'UTR of PPARA.
source: Using a luciferase reporter construct including the 3'UTR of PPARA, we revealed that MIR20B suppressed the luciferase activity in both HepG2 and Huh-7 cells in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data.

claim: The inhibitory effect of MIR20B on luciferase activity was completely blunted when using the mutant construct of the predicted MIR20B-binding sites within the 3'UTR of PPARA.
source: Furthermore, we built the mutant construct of the predicted MIR20B-binding sites within the 3'UTR of PPARA; the inhibitory effect of MIR20B on luciferase activity was completely blunted (Figure 2L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figures 2L and 2M.

claim: MIR20B significantly suppressed the expression of PPARA and its target genes in PPARA-3'UTR WT expressing cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C, MIR20B significantly suppressed the expression of PPARA and its target genes in PPARA-3'UTR WT expressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C.

claim: MIR20B increased the intracellular lipid content in PPARA-3'UTR WT expressing cells.
source: Furthermore, Oil Red O staining showed that MIR20B increased the intracellular lipid content in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: MIR20B did not have an effect on either the expression of PPARA and its target genes or the intracellular lipid content in PPARA-3'UTR Mut expressing cells.
source: However, MIR20B did not have an effect on either the expression of PPARA and its target genes or the intracellular lipid content in PPARA-3'UTR Mut expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5B-D.

claim: MIR20B inhibits the expression of PPARA by interacting with its 3'UTR.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that MIR20B inhibits the expression of PPARA by interacting with its 3'UTR.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including luciferase assays and expression studies.

claim: Transfection of MIR20B into HepG2 cells reduced the expression and activity of PPARα, but co-transfected PPARA expression vector restored them.
source: Transfection of MIR20B into HepG2 cells reduced the expression and activity of PPARα, but co-transfected PPARA expression vector restored them (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Overexpression of MIR20B reduced the expression of genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake, including CPT1A, ACOX1, CD36, and FABP1, but not de novo lipogenesis such as SREBF1 and FASN.
source: Overexpression of MIR20B reduced the expression of genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake, including CPT1A, ACOX1, CD36, and FABP1, but not de novo lipogenesis such as SREBF1 and FASN, which was significantly restored by the forced expression of PPARα (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ectopic expression of anti-MIR20B increased the expression and activity of PPARα.
source: Ectopic expression of anti-MIR20B increased the expression and activity of PPARα (Figure 3D and E), and consequently enhanced the expression of genes involved in FA utilization and oxidation (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D, 3E, and 3F.

claim: PPARA-targeting siRNA (siPPARA) suppressed the expression of PPARA and its activity.
source: PPARA-targeting siRNA (siPPARA) suppressed the expression of PPARA and its activity (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The increased expression of genes by anti-MIR20B was suppressed by siPPARA.
source: The increased expression of genes by anti-MIR20B was also suppressed by siPPARA (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Fenofibrate, a PPARα agonist, increased the expression of PPARα and its transcriptional activity in HepG2 cells transfected with MIR20B, but could not restore as much on its own effects.
source: In addition, fenofibrate, a PPARα agonist, increased the expression of PPARα and its transcriptional activity in HepG2 cells transfected with MIR20B, but could not restore as much on its own effects (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Fenofibrate treatment increased the expression of genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake which are regulated by PPARα, but could not overcome the inhibitory effect of MIR20B.
source: Interestingly, fenofibrate treatment increased the expression of genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake which are regulated by PPARα, but could not overcome the inhibitory effect of MIR20B (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: MIR20B affects lipid metabolism through direct inhibition of PPARA.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that MIR20B affects lipid metabolism through direct inhibition of PPARA.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing the effects of MIR20B on PPARA and lipid metabolism genes.

claim: MIR20B alone did not induce lipid accumulation in primary hepatocytes without OA treatment, but MIR20B significantly increased lipid accumulation in the presence of OA.
source: Unlike in HepG2 cells (Figure 2A–C), MIR20B alone did not induce lipid accumulation in primary hepatocytes without OA treatment, but MIR20B significantly increased lipid accumulation in the presence of OA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: The mRNA levels of genes involved in FA β-oxidation, FA uptake, including CPT1A, ACOX1, CD36, and FABP1, and PPARα target genes were decreased by overexpression of MIR20B compared to the control in HepG2 cells and primary hepatocytes.
source: The mRNA levels of genes involved in FA β-oxidation, FA uptake, including CPT1A, ACOX1, CD36, and FABP1, and PPARα target genes were decreased by overexpression of MIR20B compared to the control in HepG2 cells and primary hepatocytes (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 4A, 4B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The genes associated with de novo lipogenesis and ketogenesis were not affected by MIR20B.
source: whereas the genes associated with de novo lipogenesis and ketogenesis were not affected by MIR20B (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2E; Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: DGAT1, rate limiting enzyme for TG synthesis, was increased in HepG2 cells upon OA treatment.
source: Interestingly, DGAT1, rate limiting enzyme for TG synthesis, was increased in HepG2 cells upon OA treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MIR20B overexpressed HepG2 cells showed reduced levels of palmitoyl-carnitine, a substrate of β-oxidation, and acetyl-CoA, a product of β-oxidation.
source: MIR20B overexpressed HepG2 cells showed reduced levels of palmitoyl-carnitine, a substrate of β-oxidation, and acetyl-CoA, a product of β-oxidation. Subsequently, TCA cycle intermediate levels, including citrate and succinate, also decreased (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Enforced expression of MIR20B in HepG2 cells under both basal and OA treatments decreased the expression of PPARGC1A and SIRT1, which are involved in mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Enforced expression of MIR20B in HepG2 cells under both basal and OA treatments decreased the expression of PPARGC1A and SIRT1, which are involved in mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The copy number of two mtDNA genes, VIPR1 and MT-ATP6, was decreased by MIR20B overexpression following OA treatment.
source: The copy number of two mtDNA genes, VIPR1 and MT-ATP6, was decreased by MIR20B overexpression following OA treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mtDNA copy number data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mitochondrial function that was analyzed via OCR (oxygen consumption rate) was reduced by MIR20B under both basal and OA treatment conditions compared to the control.
source: Consistently, mitochondrial function that was analyzed via OCR (oxygen consumption rate) was reduced by MIR20B under both basal and OA treatment conditions compared to the control (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR measurement data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The basal respiration and maximal respiratory capacity were significantly suppressed by MIR20B.
source: In particular, the basal respiration and maximal respiratory capacity were significantly suppressed by MIR20B (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The level of ATP production, FA uptake, and FA oxidation was reduced in MIR20B overexpressed cells compared with that in the control under both basal and OA-treated conditions.
source: Furthermore, the level of ATP production, FA uptake, and FA oxidation was reduced in MIR20B overexpressed cells compared with that in the control under both basal and OA-treated conditions (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figures 4I-K.

claim: Anti-MIR20B remarkably decreased intracellular lipid accumulation upon OA treatment in HepG2 cells and primary hepatocytes.
source: Oil red O staining showed that anti-MIR20B remarkably decreased intracellular lipid accumulation upon OA treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Oil Red O staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A, D.

claim: MIR20B inhibition reduced the levels of both TG and cholesterol under OA conditions compared to the control.
source: As expected, MIR20B inhibition reduced the levels of both TG and cholesterol under OA conditions compared to the control (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, C, E, and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by TG and cholesterol measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, C, E, and F.

claim: Lipid consumption-associated genes and PPARα target genes, not de novo lipogenic genes, were significantly upregulated in MIR20B inhibited HepG2 cells and primary hepatocytes compared to those in the control under both basal and OA conditions.
source: Lipid consumption-associated genes and PPARα target genes, not de novo lipogenic genes, were significantly upregulated in MIR20B inhibited HepG2 cells and primary hepatocytes compared to those in the control under both basal and OA conditions (Figure 4M, Figure 4—figure supplements 1B; 4H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4M and supplementary figures.

claim: TG synthesis enzymes, such GPAT1 and AGPAT1, were decreased by anti-MIR20B in HepG2 cells under OA-treated condition, however DGAT1 and DGAT2 were reduced under both basal and OA-treated conditions.
source: TG synthesis enzymes, such GPAT1 and AGPAT1, were decreased by anti-MIR20B in HepG2 cells under OA-treated condition, however DGAT1 and DGAT2 were reduced under both basal and OA-treated conditions (Figure 4N).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Inhibition of MIR20B increased the levels of palmitoyl-carnitine, acetyl-CoA, and TCA cycle intermediates.
source: Inhibition of MIR20B increased the levels of palmitoyl-carnitine, acetyl-CoA, and TCA cycle intermediates (Figure 4O)
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite measurement data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: Ketogenesis was not affected by inhibition of MIR20B.
source: whereas ketogenesis was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression and metabolite data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The expression of mitochondrial biogenesis genes and the copy number of mitochondrial DNA genes were increased in both basal and OA conditions by anti-MIR20B treatment.
source: Furthermore, the expression of mitochondrial biogenesis genes (Figure 4P) and the copy number of mitochondrial DNA genes were increased in both basal and OA conditions (Figure 4Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression and mtDNA copy number data shown in Figures 4P and 4Q.

claim: Anti-MIR20B treatment significantly upregulated the mitochondrial activity, FA uptake, and FA oxidation.
source: Consequently, anti-MIR20B treatment significantly upregulated the mitochondrial activity, FA uptake, and FA oxidation (Figure 4R–V).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figures 4R-V.

claim: MIR20B contributes to hepatic lipid accumulation by controlling lipid oxidation, mitochondrial function and TG synthesis through changes in gene expression, further contributing to the progression of NAFLD.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that MIR20B contributes to hepatic lipid accumulation by controlling lipid oxidation, mitochondrial function and TG synthesis through changes in gene expression, further contributing to the progression of NAFLD.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing the effects of MIR20B on various aspects of lipid metabolism.

claim: Administration of AAV-Mir20b led to high expression levels of Mir20b in the livers of NCD- and HFD-fed mice compared to AAV-Control injection.
source: Administration of AAV- Mir20b led to high expression levels of Mir20b in the livers of NCD- and HFD-fed mice compared to AAV-Control injection (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The expression level of Mir20b was not changed in adipose tissues including white and brown adipose tissues compared to NCD- or HFD-fed AAV-Control injected mice, respectively.
source: However, the expression level of Mir20b was not changed in adipose tissues including white and brown adipose tissues compared to NCD- or HFD-fed AAV-Control injected mice, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: AAV-Mir20b injected mice exhibited a reduction in the expression of Ppara and PPARα target genes compared with AAV-Control injected mice on both NCD and HFD.
source: Consequently, AAV-Mir20b injected mice exhibited a reduction in the expression of Ppara and PPARα target genes compared with AAV-Control injected mice on both NCD and HFD (Figure 5B and R, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 5B, 5R, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Alterations in body weight were not detected in NCD-fed mice after AAV-Mir20b administration; however, AAV-Mir20b led to a significant increase in the body weight of HFD-induced obese mice.
source: Alterations in body weight were not detected in NCD-fed mice after AAV-Mir20b administration; however, AAV-Mir20b led to a significant increase in the body weight of HFD-induced obese mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurement data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ratio of fat mass to body weight in AAV-Mir20b administration HFD-fed mice was higher than that in AAV-Control treated mice.
source: The ratio of fat mass to body weight in AAV-Mir20b administration HFD-fed mice was higher than that in AAV-Control treated mice (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ratio of lean mass to body weight was decreased in AAV-Mir20b administration HFD-fed mice.
source: however, the ratio of lean mass to body weight was decreased (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: AAV-Mir20b administration increased liver weight, steatosis, and NAFLD activity score (NAS) in HFD-fed mice.
source: Consistently, AAV-Mir20b administration increased liver weight, steatosis, and NAFLD activity score (NAS) in HFD-fed mice (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by liver weight, histological, and NAS data shown in Figures 5F-H.

claim: The hepatic TG level, serum activities of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), markers of liver injury, were significantly increased with AAV-Mir20b administration compared with AAV-Control administration in HFD-fed mice.
source: The hepatic TG level, serum activities of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), markers of liver injury, were significantly increased with AAV-Mir20b administration compared with AAV-Control administration in HFD-fed mice (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurement data shown in Figures 5I-K.

claim: Delivery of AAV-Mir20b to HFD-fed mice significantly impaired glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity compared to the AAV-Control.
source: Additionally, we observed that delivery of AAV-Mir20b to HFD-fed mice significantly impaired glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity compared to the AAV-Control (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by glucose and insulin tolerance test data shown in Figures 5L and 5M.

claim: Fasting glucose, insulin, and homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) levels were increased in AAV-Mir20b administrated HFD-fed mice.
source: Fasting glucose, insulin, and homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) levels were also increased in AAV-Mir20b administrated HFD-fed mice (Figure 5N–P).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic parameter measurements shown in Figures 5N-P.

claim: Genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake pathways were downregulated by AAV-Mir20b compared to AAV-Control in both NCD- and HFD-fed mice, whereas lipogenesis genes were not altered in AAV-Mir20b administrated mice.
source: We observed that genes involved in FA β-oxidation and FA uptake pathways were downregulated by AAV-Mir20b compared to AAV-Control in both NCD- and HFD-fed mice, whereas lipogenesis genes were not altered in AAV-Mir20b administrated mice (Figure 5Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5Q.

claim: Mir20b could aggravate NAFLD by dysregulating lipid metabolism in a HFD-induced obesity model.
source: These results suggest that Mir20b could aggravate NAFLD by dysregulating lipid metabolism in a HFD-induced obesity model.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experimental results in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Administration of AAV-anti-Mir20b led to decrease of Mir20b in the livers of NCD- and HFD-fed mice compared to AAV-Control injection.
source: Administration of AAV-anti-Mir20b led to decrease of Mir20b in the livers of NCD- and HFD-fed mice compared to AAV-Control injection (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly increased expression of Ppara and its target genes in the livers of both NCD- and HFD-fed mice.
source: AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly increased expression of Ppara and its target genes in the livers of both NCD- and HFD-fed mice (Figure 6B and R and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 6B, 6R, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Administration of AAV-anti-Mir20b in HFD-fed mice reduced the body weight compared to that of AAV-Control administrated mice.
source: Administration of AAV-anti-Mir20b in HFD-fed mice reduced the body weight compared to that of AAV-Control administrated mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurement data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Alterations in body weight were associated with fat mass loss and reduced trend of epididymal white adipose tissue in AAV-anti-Mir20b administrated HFD-fed mice.
source: We further determined that alterations in body weight were associated with fat mass loss and reduced trend of epididymal white adipose tissue (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ratio of lean mass to body weight of AAV-anti-Mir20b administrated HFD-fed mice was increased, while the lean mass was comparable to that of the control.
source: While the ratio of lean mass to body weight of AAV-anti-Mir20b administrated HFD-fed mice was increased, the lean mass was comparable to that of the control (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: AAV-anti-Mir20b administration reduced liver weight and hepatic steatosis in HFD-fed mice than in AAV-Control mice.
source: We next observed that AAV-anti-Mir20b administration reduced liver weight and hepatic steatosis in HFD-fed mice than in AAV-Control mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by liver weight and histological data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Delivery of AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly attenuated the size and number of lipid droplets in the liver and NAS compared to AAV-Control administration in HFD-fed mice.
source: H&E and Oil Red O staining demonstrated that delivery of AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly attenuated the size and number of lipid droplets in the liver and NAS compared to AAV-Control administration in HFD-fed mice (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: Metabolic parameters were reduced in AAV-anti-Mir20b administrated mice compared with the AAV-Control administrated mice.
source: In accordance with histological changes, metabolic parameters were reduced in AAV-anti-Mir20b administrated mice compared with the AAV-Control administrated mice (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical measurement data shown in Figures 6I-K.

claim: AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity compared to the AAV-Control in HFD-fed mice.
source: Furthermore, AAV-anti-Mir20b significantly improved glucose tolerance (Figure 6L) and insulin sensitivity (Figure 6M) compared to the AAV-Control in HFD-fed mice.
